metadata.title: The Partnership Model: Capital, Time, and Profit
metadata.description: Understand why a partner’s profit share depends on the capital used and how long it was invested.
metadata.teachingApproach: Develop the capital-time model step by step; use timelines and segment ledgers; show intermediate calculations, unit and share checks, and topic-specific remedial feedback. Practice uses fresh values aligned to the approved scope.
metadata.sourceScope: R. S. Aggarwal, Quantitative Aptitude, Chapter 14: Partnership (printed pp. 476–492). Approved scope: Define partners and partnership; derive the capital-time measure from profit being proportional to the capital committed and the duration for which it is used. Distinguish simple partnership (equal durations, so capital alone sets the ratio) from compound partnership (different durations, so capital × time is compared). Explain compatible time units, capital units, positive investments, zero-duration boundaries, and why profit shares sum to total profit. Ground in Important Facts and solved examples 1–2, with objective patterns contrasting equal and unequal investment periods.

content.text: The Partnership Model: Capital, Time, and Profit: Understand why a partner’s profit share depends on the capital used and how long it was invested. This lesson builds a partnership model, explains each step, works through examples, and offers fresh practice with targeted recovery.

The Partnership Model: Capital, Time, and Profit asks you to decide what determines each person’s share or assigned amount. Understand why a partner’s profit share depends on the capital used and how long it was invested. We will build the model from the agreement, calculate a representative case, and test the result against the original conditions.

Start with the quantity the agreement actually rewards. In ordinary partnership profit sharing, that is the capital made available to the business over time. Capital and time jointly determine the weight of an investment. Write the partner or user labels and the stated basis before you choose an operation.

The core model is: each partner’s weight = capital × time invested. This follows by comparing equal units of capital-month: twice the capital for the same duration contributes twice as much, and the same capital held twice as long also contributes twice as much.

The weight is capital × months invested. Equal durations cancel, leaving the simple capital ratio; unequal durations require the full product. Keep the capital amount and its time period in separate columns first. Only multiply once the quantities use compatible units; this makes the origin of every ratio term visible.

Worked reasoning: A invests ₹40,000 for 12 months and B ₹60,000 for 8 months. Their weights are both ₹480,000-months, so the profit ratio is 1:1. Notice that the ratio comes from relative contribution, not from the order in which partners are named or from who manages the business. Preserve the labels until the final allocation.

When the total profit is known, add the reduced ratio terms to find total parts. Divide the distributable profit by those parts for one part, then multiply by the requested partner’s parts. Do not treat a ratio term itself as a rupee amount.

Use the timeline or agreement to identify intervals before doing arithmetic. Keep capital and time visible as separate columns before multiplying. If a partner’s capital changes, record the new amount only from the date it takes effect; if a time factor is common to everyone, cancel it only after forming the ratio.

A second way to check the model is to rebuild each partner’s contribution independently. Check every investment period against the business timeline and convert years to months before comparing. If the resulting ratio reverses a known relationship—for example, a larger weighted contribution receiving a smaller share—inspect the partner labels and ratio order.

Watch for this error: A partner joining later has fewer months; a partner withdrawing earlier contributes only through the withdrawal date. Another frequent slip is to use elapsed time instead of invested time. Mark the start and end of each interval; for a late entrant in a T-month business, invested duration is T minus the delay.

A useful worked check is to allocate the full pool and add the receipts. For partner i, the share is total profit × (i’s weight / all partners’ weights). This fraction must be between 0 and 1 for positive weights, and all partner fractions must sum to 1.

Translate special wording before calculation. A percentage increase may refer to original capital, a withdrawal may be partial, and an allowance may be removed before investment-based sharing. Profit allocation follows contribution over time, not the amount deposited at a single snapshot. Underline the base of each percentage and state whether the pool is original or remaining profit.

If an unknown amount or date is requested, set up the relationship before solving. Equate the capital-time products in the stated profit ratio, or write a share as its fraction of total profit. Keep unknowns tied to their partner labels and check that a date remains within the business term.

If your first answer seems wrong, revisit the model rather than repeating the arithmetic. Ask: did I use the right basis, include every interval, convert all time units, and use the right total pool? Then substitute the candidate into the original data and recompute the ratio.

For a timed exam, use a compact ledger: partner; capital in each interval; months in that interval; weighted contribution; share fraction. Reduce large products by common factors only after they are formed, and keep exact fractions until the final currency amount.

Mastery check: explain why the chosen weights represent the agreement, show one intermediate calculation, and verify the final share or sufficiency conclusion. You should now be able to solve the approved scope for the partnership model: capital, time, and profit without relying on a memorized answer pattern.
